name: Carlos Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual workday for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the cable and tools in the yard, ride out with a senior lineworker, and spend a lot of the day in a bucket tracing faults. I like the puzzle of a strange outage; I still have to check my measurements twice because a wrong size ends up on the order sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tool can turn my scrappy end-of-day notes into a readable handover, which is useful but hardly a new trade. I use it every day and still have to correct the cable sizes before anyone orders parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The crew has a backlog of ordinary repairs, and the company pays me for climbing and safe work, not elegant reports. At home my partner's library wage and mine cover the mortgage, and we've got nearly five months of bills saved, although the car is getting old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with line shifts and check each AI draft against my measurements before it goes to the stores team. From the next pay I'd put 50 a month into a car repair account rather than wait for the engine to strand us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly relaxed about this picture and even glad to spend less of the evening typing. A breakdown on the way to an early call worries me more than the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you correct recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yesterday the draft said a conductor was 35 millimetres when my note said 25. I caught the AI tool's wrong cable size before ordering, which is why I keep the written measurements under my phone case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the car a worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The starter clicks twice on cold mornings, and my partner needs the car on some library days. We can pay for a repair, but I don't want to empty the emergency account for it.

say: I would welcome **readable handovers** while checking every cable size.
I would remind coworkers that the tool does not **climb or repair**.
think: I expect the repair backlog to keep my **line hours** steady.
Our near-five-month savings cushion faces a **car repair**, but the mortgage is covered.
do: Keep taking **line shifts** and verify AI drafts against measurements.
Put **50 monthly** into a car repair account.
feel: Fairly relaxed about the job, more alert to the **old car**.
S0.quote: I caught the AI tool's wrong cable size before ordering, which is why I keep the written measurements under my phone case.
fieldNote: He uses AI **daily for handovers** while retaining his own written measurements as the source of truth.
His household has a **near-five-month cushion**, and a failing car is a more immediate concern than minor automation.

steps.text: Keep line shifts and check drafted handovers against measurements
Put 50 monthly into a car repair account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that dispatch and buying will change before our bucket work does, and the new tools need to earn trust on actual outages. The office staff who know which lane floods are worth listening to when the route software is tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the company might stop replacing office workers and expect fewer field crews to clear more faults. I'm junior, so being the person who understands the approved map could help, but it won't protect me if the roster itself shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the dispatcher for two older outage records and try the approved mapping tool against them, with my lead checking my conclusions. If it proves useful, I'd learn how to flag bad routes and seek a place on the utility's trial group; if shifts fall, I'd apply to the telecoms cable crew across town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm excited by a puzzle I can test, and uneasy for the people who built those records. My confidence falls fast if a new target turns one careful repair into three rushed ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a route fail your test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One map sends the truck to a locked gate by the rail line, while the dispatcher knows a public access track. I'd mark the gate and ask whether the software can retain that correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why telecoms cable work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've helped pull low-voltage service cable, so I have a starting point, but I would still need training. I would apply only to a paid opening and ask exactly what certificate they require.

say: I would test **dispatch routes** against actual outage records.
I would ask the company to hear **local office knowledge**.
think: I could benefit from knowing the **approved map** better than other junior workers.
I might still lose hours if **field rosters** shrink.
do: Test **two old outages** with the approved mapping tool.
Join the utility **trial group** if it proves useful.
Apply to **telecoms cable work** if shifts fall.
feel: Excited to test, yet uneasy about **rushed repairs** and office losses.
S1.quote: I'm junior, so being the person who understands the approved map could help, but it won't protect me if the roster itself shrinks.
fieldNote: His approach is experimental: compare maps with **two historical outages** and use a lead worker to check conclusions.
He sees skill with tools as useful, while acknowledging **roster risk** and the need for a paid alternative.

steps.text: Test approved mapping against two old outages with his lead
Join the utility trial group if the mapping tool proves useful
Apply for a paid telecoms cable opening if shifts fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a thinking system in 2028 could write the job tickets and buy the cable, but people still climb until capable robots arrive around 2031. I'd ask for trial access and a written plan for the workers whose jobs change at each date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 45 for the first change and 48 for the physical robots, while our children are still in school and the mortgage runs on. I could learn a new tool quickly, yet a machine that actually repairs a line could take the work that pays most of our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to observe any company robot trial and cut our holiday savings contribution until the staffing plan is clear. In 2029 I'd keep paid line shifts, practise with the approved AI job-ticket system, and submit a telecoms cable application if our crew loses days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pace scares me, even though I want to see the machine up close. I can test software on a weekend; I can't make an employer offer me another wage on demand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for at a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what happens when a crossarm is crooked and the old bolts don't line up with the drawing. A perfect training pole would tell me almost nothing about our actual network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner hear that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say our savings buy some time, but not enough to wait until the last shift disappears. My partner would probably ask whether the library's own staffing is safe, and I wouldn't know the answer.

say: I would separate **2028 job-ticket changes** from 2031 robot repairs.
I would ask for **trial access** and a written worker plan.
think: I will be **45 then 48**, with children at school and a mortgage.
Fast learning cannot replace the **line wage** if robots do the repair.
do: Observe a **robot trial** and pause holiday savings contributions.
Keep paid **line shifts** and practise the approved ticket system in 2029.
Apply to **telecoms cable work** if crew days fall.
feel: Scared by the pace but eager to **see the machine**.
S2.quote: I can test software on a weekend; I can't make an employer offer me another wage on demand.
fieldNote: He wants to inspect robot performance on **crooked old hardware**, not a neat training pole.
His partner’s **library job** could also change after thinking AI, compounding the household risk he admits privately.

steps.text: Practise the approved AI job-ticket system during 2029
Apply for paid telecoms cable work if crew days fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets the utility compare new machines with skilled crews before changing pay or staffing. I would ask for real trial results and a route for juniors like me to learn inspection and equipment control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 48 at the 2031 thinking AI date and 51 when physical robots can work on lines around 2034. The children will be older, but the mortgage doesn't care; I can't assume a robot supervisor role will exist just because it sounds sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office this year which drone inspection course it recognises and pay 50 a month into the car fund while my wages hold. If a funded seat opens, I'd take it; in 2032 I'd keep climbing for pay and apply for a paid inspection trial after I passed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keen to learn something concrete and less cornered than in the two-year picture. I still worry the utility could train twenty of us for two posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want supervised flights near wires, a clear rule for when a human climbs to confirm a defect, and practice reading images. I would not put a drone near live equipment on the strength of a short online lesson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose between trial work and line pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my regular shifts unless the trial has written hours and pay. My partner and I can discuss a risk, but we can't pay the mortgage with a promising title.

say: I would ask for **real trial results** before staffing changes.
I would seek a route for juniors into **inspection skills**.
think: I will be **48 then 51** at the two arrival dates.
The mortgage remains, and a **robot supervisor** post is not guaranteed.
do: Ask which **drone course** the utility accepts.
Fund the **car account** and enrol if a paid place opens.
Keep climbing in **2032** and apply for a paid inspection trial after qualifying.
feel: Keen to learn, with concern about **few paid posts**.
S3.quote: My partner and I can discuss a risk, but we can't pay the mortgage with a promising title.
fieldNote: He wants **supervised flights** and a rule for human confirmation before drones inspect live assets.
His enthusiasm is bounded by **written hours and pay**, not faith that a new job title will exist.

steps.text: Put 50 monthly into the car repair account
Take the recognised drone inspection course if funded
Apply for paid inspection trial work after qualifying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the yard that ten years should give us evidence, worker training and a fair way to fill the remaining posts. I'd ask for annual figures on outages and paid crew hours, because a robot trial should be judged on both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 in 2036 and 56 when capable robots arrive around 2039. Our children may have moved out by then, but I haven't checked the pension or the final mortgage date, so planning to stop work would be a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking line shifts, learn the approved inspection tools as they arrive, and use spare evenings for a funded drone course if the utility offers one. If I qualify, in 2037 I'd apply for a paid network inspection role and keep the car and mortgage reserves growing while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning makes me hopeful that I could turn my curiosity into a proper job. It also makes me impatient with vague promises, because ten years is plenty of time to show the hours and salary in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you measure each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare defects found per circuit with the number of paid crew hours and return visits. If the machine misses a fault, somebody still has to make the next safe repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work at 56 if the line role ends?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I can get paid inspection work; I would check our benefits before even thinking about retirement. I want my children to choose their own work, not inherit our mortgage plan.

say: I would ask for **annual outage and wage-hour** results.
I would want fair access to **remaining paid posts**.
think: I will be **53 and 56** at the two arrival dates.
I cannot assume grown children or an unchecked **pension** will cover the mortgage.
do: Keep **line shifts** and learn approved inspection tools.
Take a **funded drone course** if offered.
Apply for paid **network inspection** in 2037 if qualified.
feel: Hopeful about a new role, impatient with **vague pay promises**.
S4.quote: I want my children to choose their own work, not inherit our mortgage plan.
fieldNote: He frames robot performance through **defects and returns** alongside paid hours, rather than a single productivity figure.
The decade supports a **specific paid inspection path**, but he refuses to count unverified pension or family support.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts while learning approved inspection tools
Take a funded drone inspection course if offered
Apply for paid network inspection in 2037 if qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots would reach the hands-on work before I could be sure of a new paid role, and my partner's library work might change too. I'd need honest trial results, paid training seats and real vacancies with hours in writing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks the faults the robot misses. Someone has to climb after a missed defect, and that person's hours, training and safety need to be part of the plan.

headlineQuote: Someone has to climb after a missed defect, and that person's hours, training and safety need to be part of the plan.
portrait: Carlos is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with two school-age children and a mortgage shared with his partner.
He uses **AI daily** for handovers but checks cable measurements against handwritten notes.
Their savings cover nearly **five months**, with an ageing car and possible changes to his partner’s library work.
He seeks **measured trials** and funded drone training linked to paid inspection jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because line robots follow quickly and his partner’s library work may also change.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **honest trial results**, funded training seats and real vacancies with written hours.
